description: Question: which APIs bring something no other API does, and which fields are crowded with near-copies? Idea: Explore gives every API a uniqueness score (formula v1, frontend/scripts/uniqueness.py): distinct = 1 − the mean TF-IDF cosine similarity of its description to its 5 nearest APIs (title and tags counted twice, summary and description, stop words and place names removed), rarity = 1 − n/(2(n + 20)) for its least crowded category (n other APIs in it), score = 100 · distinct · rarity. This dashboard recomputes it from the public catalog on the CDN (the raw items, so it works before and after the catalog carries a uniqueness field): one JavaScript step builds the TF-IDF vectors and finds each API's 10 nearest, with place names removed and kept; everything after it (the formula for k = 3, 5 and 10, rarity, percentiles, fields, the test) is Polars. Why not Polars for TF-IDF: the tokens would be easy, but the all-pairs cosine is a self-join on shared words (one row per pair and word, millions of rows here) followed by a top-k per API, and the runtime's dialect has no rank; an inverted index in JavaScript does it in under a second. Findings on the catalog of 13 November 2026 (508 APIs): the median score is 69 (range 47–94). Rarity drives the ranking more than the text (Spearman ρ 0.76 against 0.63), and the two are almost independent (ρ 0.05): big science and engineering categories (20–30 APIs each) score low although their descriptions are distinct (≈ 0.85), while the true near-copies are vendor product lines described from one template: SportsData.io's v3 feeds, the EPA ECHO acts, OnSched, WMATA (23 APIs have a twin with cosine above 0.5). The hypothesis that energy and markets are crowded by per-country copies holds only for energy, and only a little: those 28 APIs are less distinct (0.809 against 0.832, Welch t = −2.0), and they are the group where removing place names makes neighbours look more alike (t = 2.5; Fingrid, Statnett, Elering), but the effect is a few thousandths of similarity; markets has 2 APIs, both unique. The ranking is robust: Spearman 0.985 with k = 3, 0.970 with k = 10, 0.998 with place names kept. Aha: 'unique' has two halves that measure different things, a crowded field of different APIs and a small field of copies; read the score with its nearest neighbours. Caveats: it measures the catalog's descriptions, not the data the APIs return (two APIs with the same data and different prose look unique); description length barely matters (ρ −0.09 with distinct); categories are the catalog's at fetch time, and the catalog changes as APIs are added. Next: click any API for its Explore page; drill into a crowded category in the field chart; expand by following a knot of mixed colours in the network (the same thing filed under different fields).
name: How unique is an API? A study of the Explore catalog
